qa.name: Tibialis Anterior
qa.origin: Lateral surface of the upper two-thirds of the tibia and interosseous membrane
qa.insertion: Medial cuneiform and base of first metatarsal
qa.innervation: Deep fibular (peroneal) nerve (L4, L5); primary dorsiflexor
qa.function: Dorsiflexes the ankle; inverts the foot
qa.opposing_muscle: Gastrocnemius and soleus (plantarflexion); fibularis longus and brevis (eversion)
qa.clinical_note: Tibialis Anterior is the largest and most medial muscle of the anterior compartment, and the primary dorsiflexor of the ankle. Deep fibular nerve palsy (from compartment syndrome, tight cast, or peroneal nerve injury at the fibular neck) causes foot drop — inability to dorsiflex, with a steppage gait. Anterior compartment syndrome after tibial fracture or exercise is a surgical emergency — the anterior tibial artery and deep fibular nerve are compressed, causing pain, pallor, and weakness of dorsiflexion. L4 root lesion classically affects tibialis anterior.

qa.name: Extensor Hallucis Longus
qa.origin: Middle half of the medial surface of the fibula and interosseous membrane
qa.insertion: Dorsal surface of the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe
qa.innervation: Deep fibular (peroneal) nerve (L4, L5); L5 indicator muscle
qa.function: Extends (dorsiflexes) the great toe; dorsiflexes the ankle; assists inversion of the foot
qa.clinical_note: Extensor Hallucis Longus lies between tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus in the anterior compartment. Its tendon is prominent on the dorsum of the foot with active great toe extension and is a useful landmark for the dorsalis pedis pulse (lateral to EHL tendon). EHL weakness is a sensitive indicator of L5 nerve root compression — typically from L4–L5 disc herniation. Testing great toe extension against resistance is a standard L5 neurological exam manoeuvre.

qa.name: Extensor Digitorum Longus
qa.origin: Lateral condyle of tibia, upper three-quarters of fibula, interosseous membrane
qa.insertion: Middle and distal phalanges of the lateral four toes via extensor expansion
qa.innervation: Deep fibular (peroneal) nerve (L4, L5); lateral anterior compartment
qa.function: Extends the lateral four toes; dorsiflexes the ankle; assists eversion of the foot
qa.clinical_note: Extensor Digitorum Longus is the most lateral muscle of the anterior compartment. Its four tendons fan out across the dorsum of the foot to the lateral four toes. All three anterior compartment muscles (Tibialis Anterior, EHL, EDL) share deep fibular nerve innervation (L4–L5) and are supplied by the anterior tibial artery. Foot drop from deep fibular nerve palsy affects all three — the patient cannot dorsiflex or extend the toes, causing a characteristic high-stepping steppage gait.
